name: Subscription Traps & Free Trial Scams
summary: A free trial or once-off purchase quietly enrols you in a recurring charge that is deliberately difficult to cancel.

typicalLoss.note: Charges are small enough to escape notice on a statement, which is why they often run for a year or more.

targets: Anyone who signs up for a free trial
Users of social media advertised products
People who do not review statements

howItWorks.detail: A free sample, a R10 trial, a heavily discounted first month. Card details are required 'for verification' or a small delivery charge.
The recurring charge, its amount and the cancellation window are disclosed, but in small print, behind a link, or below the fold.
Charges start at an amount below the threshold most people notice, sometimes under a merchant name unrelated to what you bought.
No cancellation in the account, support that does not respond, or a requirement to phone during limited hours. The friction is the business model.

redFlags: Card details required for something described as free.
The cancellation process is not visible before you sign up.
Terms are behind a link rather than shown at checkout.
The merchant name on your statement does not match the product.
Reviews mention difficulty cancelling. This is the single most useful thing to search for.
illustrativeCase: A social media advert offers a skincare sample for R29 delivery. The terms, in small print below the order button, enrol the buyer in a R749 monthly supply. The charges appear under an unrelated merchant name and run for fourteen months before being noticed, totalling over R10 000.
howToProtect: Search the product name plus 'cancel' before signing up for any trial.
Use a virtual card or a low-limit card for trials so you can close it easily.
Screenshot the terms at the point of purchase. You will need them in a dispute.
Diarise the cancellation date the moment you sign up.
Review your bank statement line by line once a month. Most of these survive on inattention.
ifYouveBeenHit: Cancel in writing and keep proof of the date.
Instruct your bank to stop the recurring card payment or debit order.
Dispute charges taken after your cancellation, with your screenshots as evidence.
Complain to the National Consumer Commission, since aggressive negative-option billing may breach the Consumer Protection Act.

faqs.q: Can my bank stop a recurring card payment?
faqs.a: Yes. You can instruct your bank to block future recurring payments to a merchant, and you should also cancel with the merchant directly.
It sits on a spectrum. Clearly disclosed subscriptions are legal. Hidden terms, obstructed cancellation and misleading merchant names may breach the Consumer Protection Act and are worth reporting.
